title-group.article-title: Evaluating Kelp Feedstock for Alginate-Based Materials: Physicochemical Characterization of Sodium Alginate and Aquaculture Considerations

abstract.p: Cultivated kelps are a scalable marine feedstock for renewable polymers, but regional aquaculture supply chains lack engineering benchmarks for the alginate yield and quality. Here, we apply a lower-hazard citrate-based process to quantify bioplastics-relevant alginate metrics across cultivated northeast Pacific kelps from commercial farms in British Columbia (Canada) and Alaska (USA). Ten blade biomass samples spanning five species were screened. Two samples failed to undergo phase separation after extraction and centrifugation, indicating biomass-dependent extractability as a process risk. For the remaining eight feedstocks, yields ranged from 11.95 to 26.11% (dry weight). Weight-average molar mass (M w) ranged from 36.6 to 623 kDa, with 7/8 samples exceeding 400 kDa. Uronic acid composition spanned M/G = 0.14–1.38, with variation in G/M block compositions (block fractions and block lengths) relevant to cross-linking. Multivariate analysis resolved dominant gradients linking the uronic acid composition and molar mass distributions. The studied kelps were evaluated in the context of known seasonal, tissue-specific, and environment-driven effects and climate-related stressors that can alter productivity. Collectively, these results provide a regional benchmark for lower hazard alginate production from cultivated kelps and an engineering screening framework to support consistent feedstock selection for scalable manufacturing of alginate-based films, coatings, and related bio-based materials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Efforts to develop sustainable materials have intensified as researchers work to replace petroleum-derived plastics with renewable polymers that lower environmental impact while still meeting performance demands for packaging and other high-volume uses (e.g., flexible packaging, coatings, and molded materials). −
Although bioplastics derived from terrestrial feedstocks have advanced, reliance on arable land, freshwater, and agrochemical inputs can constrain scalability and introduce competition with food systems. Marine biomass, particularly macroalgae, offer an attractive alternative feedstock. Macroalgae grow rapidly, remove excess nutrients, and fix carbon efficiently, while being cultivated without land, freshwater, or synthetic fertilizers. , Collectively, these attributes position macroalgae as a compelling platform for next-generation bioplastics and marine bioeconomies. ,

Brown macroalgae (Phaeophyceae; kelps) are a primary industrial source of alginate, a linear anionic polysaccharide composed of β-d-mannuronic (M) and α-l-guluronic (G) acid residues (uronic acids) arranged in MM, GG, and MG/GM sequences. In brown seaweeds, alginate typically comprises about 15-45% of dry biomass and varies with species, season, environmental conditions, and maturity stage. Alginate is widely evaluated for films, coatings, and hydrogel-based materials as it forms cohesive films from aqueous solution and supports composition-tunable network formation through ionic crosslinking. , Alginate commercial demand continues to expand, with global production now exceeding 30,000 metric tons annually, , and the alginate market is projected to grow from approximately USD 832.9 million in 2023 to more than USD 1.9 trillion by 2030 (CAGR 12.8%), driven by biomedical hydrogels, bioplastics, and advanced packaging. Despite this growth, industrial supply chains remain geographically concentrated. More than 97% of global seaweed cultivation occurs in Asia, and commercial alginate production is dominated by a limited set of cultivated taxa, primarily Saccharina and Undaria (Fig. ). −
This concentration can constrain regional access to alginate feedstocks and introduce supply chain vulnerability for emerging bioplastics applications that require consistent, predictable polymer specifications. , Diversifying cultivation regions and species can strengthen supply security and enable regional biomanufacturing, while also reducing reliance on monoculture-style production systems. , Such diversification helps avoid the ecological trade-offs associated with single feedstock dominance that have been observed for some terrestrial biomass supply chains. ,

sec.p:
During the initial screening of seaweed feedstocks for bioplastic production, three physicochemical attributes are of importance: extraction yield, molar mass distribution (M
w , M
n , Đ), and uronic acid sequence conformation (M/G ratio and block distribution). Extraction yield is the fundamental techno-economic metric that dictates polymer productivity, industrial throughput, and overall manufacturing costs. , The molar mass and uronic acid sequence collectively govern solution rheology and the formation of Ca2+ mediated ″egg-box″ crosslinking, which determine a material’s stiffness-ductility balance and tolerance for defects. ,,, In general, higher molar mass supports tougher materials, while greater G sequences enhance crosslink density and stiffness, while greater sequences promote flexibility and extensibility. , Viscosity and molar mass also influence film forming capacity and barrier performance, while compositional differences can affect degradation behavior under relevant end-of-life conditions. , As these attributes vary significantly based on seaweed species, harvested tissue region, and environmental conditions, they offer an opportunity for functional tailoring but also present a major hurdle for maintaining batch-to-batch consistency in large-scale manufacturing. ,

Despite the vast diversity of regional kelp, cultivated biomass has not been adequately benchmarked against the specific alginate metrics required for bioplastic production. , In the northeast Pacific, kelp species such as Macrocystis pyrifera, Saccharina latissima, Alaria marginata, Laminaria setchellii, and Nereocystis luetkeana are actively cultivated in British Columbia (BC) and Alaska. However, compositional data for brown seaweeds from these regions remain limited and primarily concern wild harvested biomass, leaving a critical knowledge gap for aquaculture-grown feedstocks. , Understanding how species identity and cultivation environment influence alginate structure is important for developing consistent feedstocks for scalable biomanufacturing. , By comparing cultivated species, this study examines relationships among uronic acid composition, block distribution, molar mass, and inherent crosslinking capacity. It was hypothesized that species- and environment-dependent variations in these structural characteristics govern alginate crosslinking and, consequently, its suitability for bioplastic film and coating applications.

In this study, we address these gaps by characterizing the physicochemical properties of sodium alginate extracted from cultivated kelp species grown along the Canadian and Alaskan coasts. We applied a greener, citrate-based extraction method tailored for bioplastic production. Compared with conventional alkaline processes, the method uses a lower-hazard chelating agent, milder processing conditions, and fewer hazardous chemical inputs, while maintaining high alginate yield and molar mass. −
Using commercially harvested blade tissues collected under routine cultivation operations, we quantify the extraction yield, molar mass, and M/G ratio across multiple cultivated species and growth locations. This dataset links cultivation conditions to both polymer productivity and structure descriptors that govern processability, enabling prioritized selection of feedstocks for formulation/film testing and within-species variability that may limit manufacturing consistency. This study also evaluates specific harvesting considerations and vulnerability to climate-driven stressors to support future cultivation and harvesting strategies for bioplastic applications. Future studies should incorporate continuous water quality monitoring, abiotic drivers, and seasonal variability of cultivated samples to enable predictive models for the alginate composition and enable more precise cultivation strategies.

sec.title: Seaweed Samples
sec.p: Cultivated brown macroalgae were obtained directly from commercial kelp farmers operating along the coastlines of British Columbia (Canada) and Alaska (USA). Five northeast Pacific species cultivated in the region were included: Saccharina latissima, Macrocystis pyrifera, Nereocystis luetkeana, Alaria marginata, and Laminaria setchellii. Kelp species identity, harvester, collection location, and harvest date are summarized in Table and Fig. . Biomass was provided according to the current farm harvest schedules. As such, the dataset is intended as an operational baseline for bioplastics-relevant feedstock screening; observed differences among samples are interpreted as screening-level variability rather than mechanistic responses to environmental drivers or optimized harvest timing. All samples consisted of blade and midrib tissue.

sec.title: Materials and Reagents
sec.p:
Sodium carbonate (anhydrous) was purchased from Bio Basic (Canada). Hydrochloric acid (36.5-38.0%, ACS grade), sodium citrate dihydrate (>99.0%), sodium hydroxide (>97.0%, ACS grade), and ethanol (95%, spectrophotometric grade) were obtained from Fisher Chemical. Deionized water (Milli-Q, 18.2 MΩ cm) was used throughout all experiments. Reference commercial sodium alginate (KIMICA Corporation (Tokyo, Japan) (M
w = 248 kDa, M/G = 1.01)).

sec.title: Sample Preparation and Storage
sec.p:
Kelp blade tissues supplied by regional harvesters (Table ) were received pre-rinsed and dried. Upon receipt, dried samples were transferred to opaque polyethylene bottles, sealed with Parafilm, and stored at −20°C in the dark until processing. Frozen, dry storage is expected to minimize oxidative and enzymatic degradation; supporting this approach, studies on polysaccharide-producing algae report that dried thalli can be stored for several years without a noticeable decrease in polysaccharide content or alginate quality, and quantitative yields from biomass stored for up to 31 months remain comparable to initial yields. −
Nonetheless, direct evidence of multi-year compositional stability for dried kelp blade tissue stored at −20°C is limited and is noted as a potential source of variability. The day before extraction, dried biomass was manually fragmented and milled using a laboratory blender to obtain 200-800 μm particles. Ground material was stored overnight at 4°C in a sealed container and extracted the following day. Extractions were performed between May and September 2025.

sec.title: Alginate Extraction
sec.p: Sodium alginate was extracted following the optimized citrate-based protocol described by Smith et al. (2026), adapted from Sterner et al. (2016, 2017), ,, selected for its reduced chemical hazard and lower carbon footprint relative to conventional alkaline extraction, and tailored for high yield and molar mass. A schematic overview of the extraction procedure workflow is provided in Fig. . Each of the kelp samples (Table ) underwent four independent extractions to quantify the within-sample batch consistency.

caption.p: Schematic of alginate extraction procedure, adapted from Smith et al. (2026).

sec.p: Ground dry kelp biomass (12 g) was mixed with 360 g of a 0.125 M sodium citrate solution, pre-adjusted to pH 9.3 ± 0.1 using NaOH (SevenCompact S220 pH meter, Mettler Toledo, Switzerland). The suspension was mixed in a New Brunswick I26 incubator shaker (Eppendorf, USA) at 49.5 °C with agitation at 150 rpm for 1 h. Subsequently, the mixture was centrifuged using a Sorvall LYNX 4000 Superspeed Centrifuge (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) at 15 000 × g for 30 min at 21 °C to separate the supernatant containing solubilized sodium alginate from the residual biomass.

The supernatant was acidified to pH 1.2 ± 0.2 with 6 M HCl to precipitate alginic acid. The precipitate was recovered by centrifugation (15 000 × g, 15 min, 21 °C), while the supernatant, containing soluble salts (Na+, Mg2+), laminarins, and fucoidan, was discarded. The alginic acid pellet was washed twice with 0.1 M HCl, followed by centrifugation (15 000 × g, 10 min, 21 °C) after each wash. The washed pellet was resuspended in 25 mL deionized water and neutralized to pH 7.5 ± 0.2 using 1 M Na2CO3, regenerating sodium alginate.

Sodium alginate was precipitated by adding anhydrous ethanol (1:1, v/v) and collected by centrifugation (15 000 × g, 10 min, 4°C). The pellet was washed twice with 70% (v/v) ethanol under identical centrifugation conditions, and the supernatants were discarded. A final centrifugation (15 000 × g, 2 min, 4 °C) was performed to remove residual solvent. The resulting pellet was oven-dried at 30 °C until constant mass was achieved, then milled using a Retsch MM 400 mixer mill equipped with a 25 mL stainless steel canister operated at 30 Hz for 30 s. The sodium alginate powder was sealed in airtight vials and stored at 4 °C. The extraction yield was calculated according to Equation . 1 Yield(%)=(Dry⁣wt.⁣of⁣extract(g)/Dry⁣wt.⁣of⁣algal⁣biomass(g))×100

sec.title: Block Distribution and M/G Ratio
sec.p: A 2% solution of dried sodium alginate was prepared in deuterium oxide (D2O) at pH 7.5 and analyzed in 5 mm NMR tubes (Sellimi, 2015). Variable-temperature Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (1H NMR) was used to determine the uronic acid composition of sodium alginate on a Bruker DMX-500 MHz instrument at 85 °C. Spectra were acquired using signal averaging across multiple scans (8 scans); thus, each spectrum represents the bulk composition of the dissolved sample. The spectra focused on the relative integrations of three resonance peaks that correspond to distinct chemical environments, and they were processed using MestReNova software (Mnova). Fractions of guluronic acid (G blocks) and mannuronic acid (M blocks), the M/G ratio, were calculated using the spectra integrations and established equations. ,

sec.title: Molar Mass Distribution
sec.p:
Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was performed using an Agilent Infinity 1260 II HPLC system equipped with two Suprema 8 × 300 mm, 10 μm columns (100 Å and 3000 Å) with HPLC grade water (8 mmol NaN3) as eluent connected to an Agilent 1260 GPC/SEC Multi-Detector Suite (MDS) consisting of a dual-angle light scattering detector, differential refractive index detector, and a viscometer. Samples were prepared in the eluent at a concentration of approximately 2.0 mg/mL and analyzed at a flow rate of 0.800 mL/min at 25 °C (injection volume = 20 μL). Triple detection was used to calculate molar mass using a dn/dc value of 0.145 mL/g via Agilent GPC/SEC software (version 2.2). Key parameters included molar mass distribution, weight-average molecular weight (M
w ), number-average molecular weight (M
n ), and Dispersity (Đ = M
w /M
n ).

sec.title: Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
sec.p: The alginate samples were analyzed by Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) to identify the chemical composition of the extracted sodium alginate. The spectra were obtained across the 4000-450 cm–1 range, using 64 scans at a resolution of 4 cm–1 with a Cary 630 FTIR spectrometer (Agilent Technologies). Commercial sodium alginate was used as a reference material to verify characteristic absorption bands.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p:
Data for extraction yields were collected using quadruplicate replicates (n = 4), while molar mass distribution was evaluated through triplicate measurements (n = 3). The uronic acid composition was established through a single NMR acquisition per biomass sample, utilizing scan averaging to ensure the results were representative of the bulk material. Extraction yield and GPC-derived molar mass values (M
w , M
n , Đ) are reported as mean ± standard deviation. To determine significant differences among kelp samples regarding yield and molar mass, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed, followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test (p < 0.05) for samples with replicate measurements. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using OriginPro to visualize multivariate patterns in alginate physicochemical properties across species and farm sources.

sec.title: Results and Discussion
sec.p: Ten cultivated kelp biomass samples spanning five northeast Pacific species were screened as candidate alginate feedstocks for bio-based plastic applications, with samples collected according to each producer’s current harvest schedule (Table ). Recovered sodium alginate was evaluated for extraction yield, molar mass distribution, uronic acid composition (M/G), and we confirmed the characteristic chemical structure of sodium alginate extracted by FTIR. By using commercially cultivated biomass under existing production practices, this study provides a representative benchmark of regional feedstocks as they would be supplied for potential industrial use. Differences in cultivation age, harvest timing, and post harvest handling may therefore have contributed to the observed variability in alginate yield and physicochemical properties.

For two of the ten samples, N. luetkeana (C) and L. setchellii (C), alginate recovery could not be completed because the biomass could not be adequately separated following citrate-based extraction. In four independent trials, including extended centrifugation, the liquid and solid phases remained poorly partitioned, preventing isolation of a distinct alginate-containing supernatant from the residual biomass (SI Fig. S1). These samples were therefore not advanced to purification or physicochemical characterization. Notably, both samples were harvested in the late summer, and the biomass can experience accelerated tissue breakdown from warmer temperatures. −
Consequently, these results highlight the need for targeted research into how tissue age and harvest windows govern the alginate integrity and industrial processability of regional cultivated seaweed feedstocks.

sec.title: Alginate Extraction Yield
sec.p: As shown in Table , mean sodium alginate yields ranged from 12.0 to 26.1% of dry biomass and differed significantly among species and among sources within the same species (p < 0.05). The highest yields were obtained from M. pyrifera (Ca) and A. marginata (V), both exceeding 24%. Yields from S. latissima ranged from 13.2 to 20.4%, showing significant variation across V, S, and N sources. This within-species variation suggests that source-specific cultivation and conditions may influence alginate yield. Significant source-dependent differences were also observed for N. luetkeana and M. pyrifera. For N. luetkeana, the V source produced lower yield (12.0 ± 0.7%) than the N source (18.5 ± 0.7%). Moreover, M. pyrifera from the Ca source produced a higher yield (26.11 ± 0.23%) than the Cb source (20.3 ± 1.0%).

sec.p: Literature-reported alginate yields for these species across different regions and extraction methods are summarized in Table . Published yields for M. pyrifera range from 15 to 35%, consistent with the values obtained in this study and with previous reports using mild chelation-based extraction in temperate regions. Reported yields for cultivated and wild-harvested S. latissima from northern Europe and North America range from approximately 10 to 22%, also aligning with the present results. In contrast, previously reported yields of approximately 22 to 23% for wild-harvested N. luetkeana from British Columbia exceed the lowest yield measured in this study. Overall, variation in alginate yield both among and within species has been associated with geographic origin, harvest season, tissue type, cultivation conditions, and extraction methodology. ,

sec.title: Visual Appearance of Extracted Alginates
sec.p: The appearance of extracted sodium alginate powders varied among species (Fig. ). Compared with the commercial sodium alginate reference, all cultivated samples exhibited higher pigmentation, ranging from off-white to brown. S. latissima and A. marginata produced comparatively lighter powders, whereas N. luetkeana and M. pyrifera yielded darker materials, characteristics that correspond to the natural color of their respective biomass. The variation in alginate color is primarily driven by the fluctuating presence of photosynthetic pigments (e.g., fucoxanthin and phycoxanthin), the seaweed tissue age, and the environmental conditions of its habitat. ,

caption.p: Color comparison of dry sodium alginate powders extracted from cultivated kelp species and commercial sodium alginate reference (KIMICA, Japan). Samples within each column correspond to the same kelp species, while letters in parentheses denote the harvest location, as defined in Table .

sec.p: Residual pigmentation may be acceptable for applications such as opaque packaging, composites, and mulch films but may limit the suitability and market value of alginate intended for transparent films or coatings. , Additional decolorization or purification steps can be completed (e.g., adsorption, solvent-based pretreatments, or mild oxidative treatment) to ensure consumer acceptability and remove residual phenolics and other contaminants. ,, These treatments must be carefully controlled as they may lead to polymer degradation. ,

sec.title: Uronic Acid Composition and Block Structure (1H NMR)
sec.p: The uronic acid composition varied across species and sites, with M/G ratios spanning 0.14 to 1.38, indicating distinct alginate structures and potential material properties (Table ). N. luetkeana samples had the greatest guluronic acid content, particularly the N source (M/G = 0.14; FGG = 0.51). In contrast, M. pyrifera (Ca) displayed the highest M/G ratio (1.38) and MM block fraction (FMM = 0.34). A. marginata exhibited intermediate composition, with a M/G ratio of 0.79. Within the S. latissima samples, the N site sample from Alaska had a higher M content and longer average M blocks (M/G = 0.94; NM® = 1.57) than the geographically proximate V and S site samples from British Columbia, which had similar compositions (M/G = 0.63–0.64).

Differences among species were also pronounced in the average G block length ( NG® ), a key structural parameter that governs cation binding affinity and the resulting gel network architecture. ,
NG® values ranged from 1.59 in M. pyrifera (Cb) to 5.00 in N. luetkeana (V), indicating large differences in potential junction zone formation. As cation binding occurs preferentially along greater G sequences, long G blocks are expected to increase gel strength but also increase brittleness at high crosslink density. , Block distribution analysis further revealed that N. luetkeana (V) contained predominantly homopolymeric sequences (η < 1), consistent with extended G block regions that promote rigid, highly crosslinked domains. In contrast, all other species exhibited heteropolymeric sequences (η > 1), reflecting more alternating or random M/G arrangements that typically produce materials with moderate stiffness and enhanced flexibility.

The M/G ratios measured for S. latissima were consistent with ranges previously reported in Swedish studies, and the high M content of M. pyrifera agreed with trends commonly reported for this species. Reports for A. marginata alginate sequence metrics remain limited, and the present dataset provides a first benchmark for cultivated samples. A notable difference from the literature was observed for N. luetkeana; both samples observed in this study had low M/G ratios, below previously reported wild harvested populations from British Columbia (M/G ratio = 1.4).

sec.title: Molar Mass Distribution (GPC)
sec.p: Alginate molar mass characteristics differed significantly among species and harvest sites (Table ). M. pyrifera (Cb) had the highest values for weight average molar mass (623 ± 99 kDa) and number average molar mass (556 ± 92 kDa). The M w was statistically comparable to S. latissima (S) and S. latissima (N) samples (p > 0.05). All three S. latissima samples also produced high molar mass alginate, with M w values ranging from 478 to 573 kDa. The S site sample had the lowest dispersity among all samples (1.04 ± 0.01), indicating a comparatively uniform distribution of polymer chain lengths. A. marginata (V), N. luetkeana (N), and M. pyrifera (Ca) had moderate molar mass distribution, with average M w values ranging from 422 to 468.6 kDa. Among these samples, A. marginata (V) exhibited the broadest molar mass distribution (1.34 ± 0.05). In contrast, N. luetkeana (V) had a significantly lower M w (37 ± 9 kDa) than all other samples (p < 0.05). It is important to note that the GPC/SEC method separates polymers by hydrodynamic volume. For alginate, hydrodynamic behavior is influenced by chain conformation and block composition, where stiffer, more extended GG sequences may occupy a larger hydrodynamic volume than more flexible MM or alternating MG sequences. ,, Differences in M/G composition may therefore contribute to variation in the apparent molar mass measured among samples.

sec.p: Published weight-average molar mass data remain limited for the kelp species examined, particularly A. marginata and N. luetkeana (Table )­. The M w values measured for S. latissima are within the broad range reported for Swedish samples (404-1179 kDa). For M. pyrifera, the values exceed most reported values for wild harvested samples from British Columbia and Argentina (56-297 kDa) but are comparable to a previous citrate-extracted British Columbia cultivated sample (508 kDa) and lower than the value reported for commercial alginate (719 kDa). No M w data were identified for A. marginata or N. luetkeana; therefore, the values reported here provide initial benchmarks for cultivated biomass of these species.

sec.title: Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR)
sec.p: FTIR spectroscopy was employed to verify the chemical structure of the extracted alginates and confirm the presence of functional groups characteristic of sodium alginate, with reference to commercial sodium alginate (Fig. ). Spectra were collected over the range of 2000-600 cm–1, shown in Fig. .

caption.p: FTIR spectra of sodium alginates extracted from the investigated brown seaweeds and the sodium alginate commercial standard (Kimica, Japan).

sec.p:
The spectra of extracted alginates are very similar to the commercial standard showing similar positions of the characteristic bands. All samples displayed the characteristic sodium alginate asymmetric and symmetric carboxylate (O–C–O) stretching peaks at approximately 1600-1610 cm–1 and 1400-1428 cm–1, respectively. −
The strong band at 1025-1030 cm–1 reflected C–O stretching within the polysaccharide backbone, while characteristic carbohydrate peaks are shown in the anomeric region (950-750 cm–1). ,

Variations are present in the 883 cm–1 and 813 cm–1 regions across sample, as the peak at 883 cm–1 is associated with C1–H deformation in β-mannuronic acid residues, while the peak at 813 cm–1 corresponds to mannuronic acid-associated vibrations. , The sample spectra align closely with the diagnostic peaks of the commercial sodium alginate reference, confirming alginate as the predominant polysaccharide.

sec.title: Principal Component Analysis of Alginate Properties
sec.p: Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to visualize bioplastics-relevant variables (yield, molar mass distribution, and uronic acid conformation) across the eight alginate samples (Fig. ). The first two principal components explained 85.99% of the total variance, with PC1 and PC2 accounting for 51.28% and 34.71%, respectively, supporting a two-dimensional representation of the data set (Figure S2, Table S1). Given the limited sample size, the PCA was interpreted qualitatively and was not used to establish statistically significant clusters or causal relationships.

caption.p: Principal component analysis (PC1 vs PC2) biplot showing scores (red points; kelp samples) and variable loadings (blue vectors; alginate physicochemical properties, yield).

sec.p: In the biplot, samples positioned near one another have similar overall physicochemical profiles, while separation along a principal component reflects differences in the properties associated with that axis. PC1 primarily represented variation in uronic acid composition. Higher M/G ratios, M fractions, and extraction yield were oriented in the same positive direction, indicating positive covariation, while G fraction and GG block content (FGG) oriented toward negative PC1. PC2 reflected variation in molar mass and block arrangement; higher M w, M n, and mixed GM/MG sequence content were oriented positively, while MM block content (FMM) and longer M block lengths ( NM® ), were oriented negatively. Samples positioned toward a given vector were more strongly associated with the corresponding property.

Samples from the same species did not consistently group together, indicating that the harvest site contributed to differences in their combined physicochemical profiles. The greatest within-species separation was observed for N. luetkeana, whose two samples differed in molar mass while positioned on the negative side of PC1 due to their high G content. The two M. pyrifera samples also separated along PC2, with the Cb sample positioned toward higher molar mass and the Ca sample toward greater MM block content and longer M blocks. The S. latissima samples showed less separation and occupied the central to upper region of the biplot, reflecting moderate uronic acid compositions with differing molar masses and mixed GM/MG sequence content. The PCA suggests that alginate results were influenced by both species identity and harvest sites.

sec.title: Structure Informed Selection of Cultivated Kelp for Alginate-Based Materials
sec.p:
This study demonstrates that cultivated kelp species from the northeast Pacific provide alginate yields and structural properties that are promising for the production of bioplastics. Extraction yield is the fundamental techno-economic lever for industrialization of alginate bioplastic production, as it dictates manufacturing throughput, unit costs, and the eventual price competitiveness of these materials against petroleum-derived plastics. , To establish reliable and scalable supply chains, feedstock selection must prioritize species that pair high extraction efficiency with rapid biomass accumulation. For example, M. pyrifera is among the highest known productivities reported for aquatic primary producers, capable of growing up to 60 cm per day under optimal conditions, , and N. luetkeana can grow up to 10 cm per day. −
Integrating alginate extraction within a zero-waste biorefinery could enhance whole biomass utilization, improving process economics and reducing waste by converting residual fractions into co-products such as bioethanol or functional sorbents. ,,

The weight-average molecular weight alginate governs solution viscosity, chain entanglement, and cohesive film formation during aqueous processing. ,, On this basis, M. pyrifera and A. marginata emerge as strong baseline candidates under northeast Pacific cultivation conditions due to high yields and high M
w , while S. latissima remains promising because it maintained consistently high M
w across sites. Prior studies report alginates above ∼300 kDa are expected to provide markedly improved mechanical integrity relative to low M
w fractions (<200 kDa). In this study, seven of the samples evaluated exceeded 300 kDa. High M
w is a critical determinant of structural integrity and thermal resistance. Aswathy et al. established that higher molecular weight enhances tensile strength and Young’s modulus as longer polymer chains facilitate more extensive intermolecular entanglement and cohesive interactions. Our previous study showed that extracts from optimized extraction methods from Macrocystis pyrifera reaching 559.5 kDa (nearly double the reference commercial grade) displayed higher thermal stability, with oxidation peaks delayed until 259°C compared to 239°C for lower M
w alternatives. In addition to films, alginate molar mass also affects fiber processing. Hao et al. showed that that high M
w alginate supports wet-spinning into high strength multifilament fibers suitable for load-bearing fabrics. The primary industrial processing challenge is rheological. Studies report that alginates with high molecular weight produce highly viscous solutions, which can impede uniform mixing and consistent crosslinking, ultimately reducing hydrogel structural integrity. ,,, Ureña et al. demonstrated that high M
w formulations exhibit greater viscosity during film casting, which can act as a significant bottleneck for industrial-scale processability. Molar mass can be tailored through tuning processing conditions or blending during material formation. Our previous study utilized Response Surface Methodology (RSM) to achieve a ninefold increase in the Mw of M. pyrifera extracts by controlling the process conditions of the alginate extraction step, adjusting sodium citrate concentration, extraction time, and temperature. Furthermore, introducing a bimodal (binary) molar mass distribution, by combining high and low M
w alginate, can increase elastic modulus substantially without the drawback in initial solution viscosity. , Complementary formulation strategies, including the addition of low molar mass plasticizers (e.g., glycerol, sorbitol, polyethylene glycol), can further improve processability. ,

Uronic acid sequence composition provides a second selection criterion as G and M block distributions control cation affinity, junction zone density, and the stiffness-ductility balance of alginate networks. ,, Greater G compositions (low M/G; high FGG) promote dense egg-box junction formation, higher modulus, and improved barrier performance but can reduce flexibility and increase brittleness when crosslink density is high. ,,, Conversely, greater M compositions (high M/G) tend to form softer, more extensible networks, supporting applications where conformability and elongation are prioritized, such as coatings and wound dressings. −
Moreover, higher M content and alternating MG, GM sequences are more conformationally flexible than greater G alginates, which tend to increase film stretchability and reduce the glass transition temperature (T g). , Notably, however, alginates with high M block content can be less responsive to plasticization than materials with greater G content, as folded G block conformations more effectively entrap plasticizer molecules. The broad range in M/G observed here (0.14-1.38) and with differences in G and M block length and sequence distribution provides a screening framework for aligning feedstocks with target functions or applications. For example, materials requiring stiff and high barrier-oriented films are more consistent with higher G compositions (e.g., the low M/G observed in N. luetkeana (N)), whereas flexible or water-retentive films and coatings are better supported by compositions with greater M content (e.g., M. pyrifera (Ca)). Intermediate uronic acid compositions in S. latissima and A. marginata suggest broader applicability across semirigid and moderately flexible applications, with final properties tunable through crosslinking conditions and formulation strategies (e.g., plasticizers or composites).

sec.title: Aquaculture Feedstock Considerations for Alginate Bioplastic
sec.p: The differences among species and harvest sites observed in this study are consistent with previous reports of variation in the alginate content and structure. Alginate properties are influenced by light availability, nutrient concentrations, seawater temperature, and hydrodynamic exposure, resulting in spatial and temporal variation within species. , Consequently, alginate quality can differ substantially even within the same species across habitats. , This section therefore summarizes relevant physicochemical trends in the literature reported for the kelp species examined in this study and considers how they may inform biomass selection and harvest strategies for bioplastic applications.

For northeast Pacific kelps, Rossell et al. reported seasonality in wild samples; alginate content in M. pyrifera fronds (formerly M. integrifolia) and N. luetkeana blades was highest from May-August and lowest in winter. Ash content, the inorganic residue remaining after ignition (complete oxidation of organic matter), also varies strongly with season, with higher values in winter and lower values in summer. Reported ash contents are higher in N. luetkeana blades than in M. pyrifera fronds, and in both taxa, stipes contain ∼25% more ash than blades. Late spring to summer kelp typically has peak alginate concentrations while also reaching their minimum ash levels, largely due to reduced seasonal accumulation of inorganic minerals (e.g., potassium). ,, The reduction of ash content could improve demineralization during acid pre-treatment, lowering mineral interference and supporting higher extraction yields. ,

Analyzing uronic acid composition across thallus sections and tissue ages could enable targeted selection of biomass with application-specific alginate properties. In wild M. pyrifera populations from New Zealand, the alginate content in blade is highest in young tissue and decreases as the macroalgae matures. While M/G ratios in the blades decrease as they age, stipes maintain relatively high M/G ratios and stable alginate levels regardless of the seaweeds size, age, or harvest timing. , These findings highlight younger blades and stipes as optimal fractions for applications prioritizing the production of flexible materials with a high M content.

In general, reported alginate structure varies seasonally, and it shifts in uronic acid composition reflecting the physiological transitions that occur across the kelp growth cycle. , As these shifts reflect interacting effects of developmental stage and site conditions (temperature, irradiance, nutrient availability), harvest timing becomes a key lever for managing biomass quality. Swedish cultivation studies demonstrate that deployment and harvesting windows can be tuned to target specific compositional outcomes. For example, a March harvest yielded alginate with higher mannuronic acid content relative to a May harvest, and early autumn deployment followed by late spring harvest at shallow depth (∼2 m) increased glucose content while reducing ash. However, high latitude cultivation, epibiont biofouling (e.g., bryozoans, hydroids) intensifies rapidly from late spring into summer, narrowing the harvest window. −
As a result, S. latissima intended for high-value applications is typically harvested prior to severe fouling, even if later harvest could further increase carbohydrate content.

sec.title: Environmental Constraints on Feedstock and Scaleup
sec.p: Changing environmental conditions, such as seawater temperature, nutrient availability, and storm exposure, may reduce the long-term consistency of alginate feedstocks by altering biomass productivity and polymer characteristics. Scalability therefore depends on maintaining a stable and resilient cultivated biomass supply, in addition to achieving suitable alginate quality. This is increasingly important as wild and farmed kelp populations are impacted by climate-driven stressors and local ecological pressures that can affect kelp availability and quality. ,

Many kelp vulnerabilities are anthropogenically driven, including increased sedimentation and pollution and climate stressors such as more frequent marine heatwaves and prolonged El Niño conditions that suppress upwelling and reduce nutrient supply. −
Thermal stress is a key constraint on kelp supply as it can directly suppress growth, weaken tissues, impair reproduction, and increase mortality, with thresholds that vary across species and regions. ,−
Species with relatively narrow thermal margins are therefore expected to show greater production volatility as the frequency and duration of warm anomalies increase. ,

Among the species considered here, M. pyrifera exhibits comparatively broad thermal tolerance and evidence of regional adaptation across latitudes. Southern California and Baja California populations have been reported to withstand short-term exposure of approximately 24-26°C, , whereas populations from southern Chile show upper limits closer to ∼15-18°C. , Within the Northeast Pacific, M. pyrifera typically occupies cooler regimes, with northern populations most frequently observed around ∼6-11°C and southern populations around ∼13-15°C. In contrast, N. luetkeana persists primarily within temperate waters (∼4-15°C), , with maximum growth reported near ∼11.9°C and temperatures approaching ∼18°C associated with sporophyte mortality. ,
A. marginata shows a similar growth optimum near ∼11°C and upper thermal tolerance generally reported between ∼15-17°C. S. latissima typically exhibits optimal growth around ∼10-15°C, while sustained exposure above ∼15-18°C has been associated with reduced growth, tissue degradation, and increased mortality, and near complete mortality has been reported at ∼23-24°C. ,,

Furthermore, warmer surface waters increase stratification, leading to reduced vertical nutrient transport, which can limit productivity even within physiological temperature ranges. In addition, ocean warming has been associated with increased grazing pressure from herbivorous fish and sea urchins, contributing to kelp forest decline through top-down control. , In the Northeast Pacific, these dynamics were exacerbated following sea star wasting disease, which coincided with elevated ocean temperatures and caused severe declines in sunflower sea stars (Pycnopodia helianthoides), a key predator of sea urchins. ,, The resulting trophic cascade has been associated with extensive kelp loss, particularly during the 2014-2016 marine heatwave, when sea star mortality and local thermal conditions were strongly associated. ,,

In addition to climate stress, aquaculture intensification has been associated with additional localized ecological pressures, including the spread of disease, genetic interactions with wild populations, competition for nutrients, increased benthic shading, introduction of non-native species, and alterations to food web structure. ,−
These impacts have been documented in regions with intensive kelp farming, including China and the Republic of Korea, where large-scale cultivation has been connected with measurable effects in surrounding marine ecosystems. , From an aquaculture perspective, these risks support precautionary scaling approaches that emphasize species diversification (using local strains), spatial planning to access site capacity, adaptive farm management, and routine monitoring of key environmental drivers and conservation protocols. ,,

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p:
This research establishes a regional physicochemical benchmark for sodium alginate isolated from five underexplored cultivated kelp species in the northeast Pacific, utilizing a low hazard citrate-based extraction process. Evaluation across multiple aquaculture sites revealed extraction yields ranging from 12.0% to 26.1% dry weight; the highest productivity was observed in M. pyrifera (Ca) and A. marginata (V) (∼24%), while N. luetkeana (V) yielded the lowest recovery (∼12%). Uronic acid composition varied widely among feedstocks, with M/G ratios spanning 0.14 to 1.38 alongside diverse block-length metrics, indicating highly varied ionic crosslinking potential and diverse stiffness-flexibility profiles. Molar mass differed strongly among samples, but most met a film-relevant threshold; seven of the eight alginates extracted exhibited M
w greater than 300 kDa, whereas N. luetkeana (V) exhibited very low M
w (∼37 kDa).

By characterizing the physicochemical properties of alginates and determining the yield from cultivated northeast Pacific kelps, this research enables the strategic selection of feedstocks for advanced material applications, thereby fostering a sustainable regional bioeconomy. To ensure manufacturing consistency and enhance the predictability of feedstock attributes, future studies must establish precise correlations among cultivation environments, harvest timing, and resulting chemical yields and composition. These efforts are fundamental to developing resilient regional supply chains capable of supporting the scalable production of sustainable bioplastics.
